resumen: What to do when the light comes from behind: show the subject or turn it into a silhouette.

bloques.alt: Two photos of a person with the sun behind them. On the left, the light is measured for the subject: the person looks fine, but the sky turns white, blown out: 1, for the subject. On the right, it is measured for the sky: the sky keeps its colors and the person becomes a dark silhouette: 2, for the sky.
bloques.pie: 1 Measured for the subject: visible, but the sky blows out. 2 Measured for the sky: dark silhouette and colorful sky.

bloques.texto: With the light behind the subject, the camera gets confused: you decide whether you want to see the subject or the sky.

When the light comes from behind, the camera measures the bright background and the subject comes out much darker. You have two paths: expose for the subject (the sky goes white, blown out) or expose for the sky (the subject becomes a silhouette).
If you want to see the subject

items: Measure on their face with spot [[medicion|metering]]; on many phones, tap their face on the screen.
Or raise the exposure [[compensacion|compensation]], for example +1 or +2: the subject gets brighter, but so does the background.
Bounce light onto the subject with a reflector (or something white that works as one) or add a gentle flash: it fills their shadows.
Put on the [[parasol|lens hood]] so the sun doesn't add haze or light spots to the photo.
Put the subject in front of something very bright, like a sunset sky.
Measure on the sky; on many phones, tap the sky and lower the brightness.
Pick a clear shape and keep figures apart so they don't merge. A simple background, like a clear sky, leaves the shape alone.
If it isn't black enough, lower the exposure a little more.

bloques.texto: With a low sun, at sunrise or sunset, backlight is stronger and more dramatic. With a high sun it is less noticeable.
At sunset, put someone (or an object) with the sun behind them. Take one photo measuring on their face and another measuring on the sky. Compare.
